If you use the same code more than twice, write a function --> helps prevent mistakes 

Function takes inputs, does something, and returns a result. Goal is to abstract some process 

* For computations or operations you define and need to repeat, write function with arbitrary arguments etc 

Consists of: 

* arguments (inputs)
  * what goes in to your function, these get used by the code in the body (eg. x in mean(x))
  * can take default values, which define a function's input until a user overwrites them (eg. na.rm =     FALSE in mean(x))
  * names matter, use reasonable things 
  * common names: x, y for vectors. df for data frames. n for number of rows/sample size 
* body (cody that does stuff)
  * do what you want 
  * common structure is: 
    * data/input checks using conditional execution 
    * perform operations 
* return objects (what the function produces)
  * implicit (last value produced) vs. explicit (use return())
  * single value or collection of values 
  * named or unnamed 
  
Scoping: how R looks for variables 

* global environment is interactive workspace where variables are defined --> usually don't want your functions using stuff in your global environment 

Conditional execution 

* sometimes you only want to do something if a condition is met --> conidtional 
* follows basic logic rules (if, else if)

Writing functions 

* start small and avoid unnecessary complexity 

```{r message = F}
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)

set.seed(1)
```

## Functions

Start small with Z scores 

```{r}
x_vec = rnorm(n = 40, mean = 12, sd = 63)

(x_vec - mean(x_vec)) / sd(x_vec)
```

Turning it into a function: 

```{r}
z_scores = function(x) {
  
  z = (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)
  
  return(z)
  
}
```
Inside the function, depend on variable function defines (x in this case). z only exists inside the function 

Does this actually work?

```{r eval = F}
z_scores(x_vec)
z_scores(rpois(4000, lambda = 12))

z_scores(iris) #doesn't work if you don't plug in numeric vector 
z_scores(c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)) #this works, converts it to 0s and 1s - update function so this does not work in function 
```
Gives same collection of numbers as first code chunk, this probably works. Set to false so it won't break knitting.  

```{r}
z_scores = function(x) {
  
  if (!is.numeric(x)) {
    stop("Input x must be numeric")
  } else if(length(x) < 5) {
    stop("x should have 5 or more numbers")
  }
  
  z = (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)
  
  return(z)
  
}
```

## Mean and SD

```{r}
mean(x_vec)
sd(x_vec)
```

Write a function that returns mean and sd of an input vector 
```{r eval = F}
 mean_and_sd = function(x) {
  
  return_df = 
    tibble(
      mean = mean(x),
      sd = sd(x)
    )
  
  return(return_df)
}
```

Check that it works
```{r}
mean_and_sd(x_vec)
```

Making a new folder and R script and paste function in there --> easier to keep track of functions in separate folder, don't put functions in main Rmd usually. insert roxygen skeleton 

```{r}
source("source/mean_and_sd.R")
```

## Another function 

```{r}
sim_df = 
  tibble(
    x = rnorm(n = 40, mean = 12, sd = 3)
  )

sim_df |> 
  summarize(
    mean = mean(x), 
    sd = sd(x)
  )
```
function in new R script. mu = true population mean, sigma = true population SD 


```{r}
source("source/sim_mean_sd.R")
```

```{r}
sim_mean_sd(n_obs = 40, mu = 12, sigma = 3) 

sim_mean_sd(40, 12, 3)
```
R uses positional matching if you put numbers in right order 

Can use default values in R script, set function 'sim_mean_sd = function(n_obs, mu = 12, sigma = 3) {' and then can just enter one value into function call, and R will automatically assume the number is for n_obs
